So, you know, I frankly concede it has a level of remoteness from the case, Your Honour. I have to say that. But because of its potential relation with the other document, which was clearly directly relevant and was his document, I offer to tender it on that basis. And that's why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we see this document is not relevant to this witness; although, this document has gone through his unit or organisation. So this document is not admitted into the evidence at this stage, but in the future the party could resubmit it for the admission. It is so decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There's just one area I wish to ask the witness about. Re-examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is, in cross-examination, my colleague Mr. Morrissey asked you about whether you had heard any -- if you had any information connecting members of the Presidency, specifically Alija Izetbegovic, with the 10th -- Caco and the 10th Brigade in October 1993. And then he showed you a document, which is Exhibit D259. And that particular document --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise, I -- we have -- let me just explain the real problem here because -- we can only put one document up at a time. We -- sometimes they come up and down. We have one up and the other one goes, and I've just -- looking at the other one -- so I've just got a quote from it so I've just got to raise the document up again. I apologise far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You don't have a hard copy at your hands?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, no, because we only see them when they flash across the screen in front of us for the first time during cross-examination. It's extraordinarily difficult to -- to deal with multiple documents on a screen which are being tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Working out where they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Defence furnish a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think this is the document. That's -- yes. Your Honours, could I just point out that this was admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrissey, for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rather than go into private session, I'd just ask you, Witness F: I take it you recall the document which -- which you signed the 21st of October, 1993 and which you referred to obtaining "uncorroborated information that the president, Alija Izetbegovic, Caco, and some other persons from the Union of Veterans attended a meeting a few days ago t source did not know where the meeting was held. The source alleges that, among other things, the meeting discussed the need to form a Green Berets independent brigade which would be under Alija Izetbegovic's direct jurisdiction. At that meeting Izetbegovic" - a huge question mark in the margins - "organised" -- sorry, "appointed Caco commander of the brigade." And on the side is handwritten: "This should be checked." Do you recall the questions Mr. Morrissey put to you about that particular document and your -- your response a little bit earlier when you said you weren't aware of information connecting the president with the 10th at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm, of course, paraphrasing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, it's -- my friend's paraphrasing actually is a bit ambiguous because I think the witness's comments were a little -- I don't want to make a speech about this. I think -- I think it would be best not to paraphrase and perhaps put the direct issue that -- Your Honours, I'm being asked to slow down and I should probably slow down and be quiet as well. But that was potentially ambiguous, so I'd ask that perhaps the direct quote be put if my friend wants to re-examine on something that has to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe you could ask this question one by one. I also see it as a compound question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. I've just got to find the exact -- the exact passage. It's at page 41.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey questioned you about the -- the document, and a previous answer you'd given to him about your awareness of the mentioning of the name of the president this connection with the assault company. And he said: "Now, do you stand by the answer?" And your answer was: "Yes, I stand by that answer. I personally was never aware that there was any connection between the name of the president and any of those units. There is a difference in the date. The first date was the 9th of October and the date here is the 21st of October. That means the events unfolded very quickly." Now, I'm just asking you: Do you remember -- the first question: Do you remember being asked those questions and your response?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember these questions. If this is the original interpretation of my reply, then there's something wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At least, it isn't clear to me. Only the 1st of September is mentioned and some other date, without any explanation as to what this refers to. May I clarify this now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could perhaps assist you. The way it works is it's translated into English and then it's been translated back another two times, so it's quite possible that in the translating several times backwards and forwards some of the meaning from your original answer may have been lost, but that's not what I'm getting at. What I want to ask you about is the difference between your -- if there is any difference between your recollection when Mr. Morrissey first asked you about your recollection of any connection or knowledge of any connection between Caco, assault units, and the president and what you've written in this document, where you've called it "uncorroborated information which should be checked." I just want you to explain the difference there, if you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only said that I didn't remember that the president had anything to do in any way with a particular unit, that is, the 10th Mountain Brigade or any other brigade. I am not aware that the assault company or whatever its name was, was established at that time. As far as I know, it was established much earlier and it was part of the 10th Mountain Brigade. When these two things are connected in this note, what I said was that the information was unverified, that these were rumours that reached us in the course of our work, and that this was preliminary information which had to be carefully checked in great detail if it was to be considered reliable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Besides this, I think that at that time an order may already have been written on the replacement of Musan Topalovic about his dismissal from the post of brigade commander. I don't know what the date was, but when this official note was compiled, the planning of the Trebevic action was already well underway and, of course, the president knew of it because it was done with his approval. In principle, this could not have been done without him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The official note which you signed is dated the 21st of October, 1993, and today is the 9th of March, 2005. When was the last time you saw that document in which you refer to "uncorroborated information" which needed to be checked about the Presidency between the 21st of October, 1993 and today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably only when I wrote it. I never saw it again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the state of your memory about the contents of that document when Mr. Morrissey asked you about the president, Izetbegovic, and any connection with the 10th and the assault units before showing you that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I can say is, with respect to the president, to the best of my knowledge he had nothing to do with these assault units. These units were subordinated to their brigades and these brigades were subordinated to the 1st Corps. It would not have been logical for the president to communicate with these units directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what I'm getting at is the state of your memory as to the contents of the documents. Now, Mr. Morrissey asked you about the contents of the document before showing it to you. What was your -- what was the state of your memory about the information in the document, that is, about uncorroborated information that needed to be checked about -- concerning the president before -- when Mr. Morrissey asked you that, before he showed you the document a little bit later?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I object to that. That's not what happened. I questioned him about the other document, the one which wasn't admitted into evidence. And then when he gave those answers, I then -- and the Court will easily remember this, because it was when the computer froze. I then had the other document, which I then sought to show him straight away. And then we had a break and we then went into that document. What he was questioned about in substance before putting the document was the material -- was the matters concerned with the 9th of October, the earlier materials, if you like, and then that document was put to him. But his answer was that he hasn't seen it. And Your Honours have ruled on that document. I think my friend may be confused about that course. But, in any event, the -- the -- the question is misleading, so I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I did not see any merits in your question, Mr. Re, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: On the basis that I was confused as to which document Mr. Morrissey had been asking the witness about, I accept that -- I'll accept what Mr. Morrissey says. I'm not -- I'm not quibbling with that. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage, are there any documents to tender? Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, but could I just indicate that the document D263, which was tendered earlier, which is the removal of Mr. Halilovic from his position. And I said it was -- I think it was -- I thought it was a Prosecution exhibit. It's actually an extract from Prosecution -- 65 ter number 83. It's the third paragraph in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And how about the document P216? Are you going to tender it or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I thought it was tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was it MFI or P? I thought it was P. If I'm wrong -- the case manager tells me it's got a P number, not an MFI number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, P16.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: 216. My information is --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, my information is that it is tendered because it has a P number. If it had an MFI number, it hasn't been tendered. It's marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I have it as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So it's admitted already. Yes. On the part of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I'm sorry. I'm now lost in the numbers, I'm sorry to say. MFI -- would Your Honour just excuse me? I just want to seek an explanation of something. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. There's MFI255, which I seek to tender. That's the document dated 1st of July coming from the 1st Corps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I -- I think we have already made decisions on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Is that one ruled upon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I just asked you whether you had other --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. My notation system. Through my fault there. And I think MFI262 remains to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: 262 is admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I have no other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. When Madam Usher pulls down the blinds, she will show you out of the room. We wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, do we have the next witness? Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, the next witness is Mustafa Kadic. No protective measures have been sought nor ordered. My learned colleague Mr. Sachdeva will take him in his evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you going to introduce the next witness through the Rule 89(F)?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'll be taking his evidence live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, your witness, please. Examined by Mr. Sachdeva:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you state your name, your date of birth, and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Mustafa Kadic. The 15th of September, 1957 in Ustibar [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you some questions about your personal background.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I'll be leading the evidence from the witness, with your leave, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a former soldier in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the JNA, 1978, when I did my military service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You served in the first aid unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, in the medical corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1991, you completed professional -- further professional qualifications in metalwork, is that right, in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before the beginning of the war, you lived in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in spring 1992, you joined the territorial army unit in Alipasino Polje; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this unit was called the Stela Unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, you were transferred to the Kosovo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is where you presently work; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the beginning of 1993, did you join the 2nd Independent Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which unit or company of that battalion were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: This was the 2nd Independent Battalion, the 3rd Company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the 3rd Company?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Senad Sakovic was the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court who was the commander of the 2nd Independent Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Adnan Solakovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And within which corps was the 2nd Independent Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: The 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Karavelic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your role in the 3rd Company of the 2nd Independent Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: I was a private.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where mostly were you situated within that company? Where did you actually do your activities?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand. When we were --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, were you based on the front lines? Sorry, my fault.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were at the front lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to take you to September 1993. Were you deployed anywhere outside of Sarajevo at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: In early September 1993, we were deployed in Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who deployed you there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: We were simply told to go there, you know. We didn't know who deployed us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who told you to go there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: It was the company commander, when he returned from a meeting with the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "company commander," you mean Senad Sakovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what he actually said to you? Did he give you the purpose of your deployment to Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: He told us we were going to Herzegovina, that there was some combat operations there, and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you what kind of combat operations there would be there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Not initially. Not when we were about to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find out later what kind of combat operations they were going to be?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Yes, later, when we were supposed to leave Grabovica, that's when we were told we were to take some positions that were being held by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll get to that later, sir, but can you tell us: When you were told about your particular operations, did you know if it was part of a larger military operation?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Who did you go with when you were deployed to Herzegovina in early September 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Am I supposed to tell you the names of the people I went with?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can, yes, please. Well, firstly, were they part of your company?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was Senad Sakovic, the company commander; Sahat Sadik, Mustafa Karic, Zdenko Jelusic, Elmedin Spaho. Those are the names I can remember right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you go to Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: From Sarajevo to Hrasnica, we went on foot. Then we got onto trucks, and we were brought to Herzegovina by truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many trucks did you travel in?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Three trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date of your arrival in Grabovica, roughly?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Only that it was early September. I couldn't recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Grabovica, do you -- can you recall roughly the time period when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: A little after noon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about your arrival in Grabovica. When you got there, did you see any other soldiers in the village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you see there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, there was no one in the village. But later on we saw civilians. At the time of our arrival, we didn't observe anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say later on you saw civilian, could you please tell the Court which ethnicity those civilians were.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Croats. They were Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from the Croat civilians and -- and yourselves, did you see anybody else in the village while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: On the first day? Or during our stay?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay, yes.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: On the second day, a unit arrived, Ramiz Delalic's unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'll -- I'll get back to that episode in a bit. Well, okay, tell us about these civilians. When did you meet these civilians?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: We were billeted in houses when we got down there. They sent us to a house, and a lady arrived in the garden of that house to gather some vegetables, and then she told us that this was her garden and that the house in which we were billeted belonged to her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally speak to her?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe her for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: She was between 40 and 50 years old. She had short fair hair. And she was wearing a dress. I can't remember the colour. It was a short-sleeved dress, because the weather was warm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she have any weapons on her?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally speak to her?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did she say to you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: When she told us it was her house, we asked her why she wasn't at home in her house, because she said that she was staying with some other people in another house. Then she said to us that she didn't have things in her house and that she had moved into another house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "things in her house," what do you mean by that exactly?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Well, usually there are some things in a house; whereas, in this house there was no furniture. The rooms were bare. There was nothing in them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If she did or not, did she tell you anything about what happened to those things in her house?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: We did ask her why there were no things in there, and she said that some soldiers had taken it away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she tell you which soldiers had taken them away?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: When we asked her, she didn't reply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know at that time under whose control was the village of Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Under the control of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, apart from this lady that you've told us about, who else did you see at the village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: I saw another old man. He was standing farther away. However, I didn't talk to him. I simply saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what this old man looked like?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Well, an older man, between 70 and 80 years old, walking with a cane, dressed in typical rural clothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during your stay in the village -- and I'll actually ask you to point out where you stayed from a photograph which I'll show you later. But for now apart from the soldiers, the military personnel that you talked about and the Croatian -- the Croat civilian, did you see any other people in the village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: In the village, an elderly man came to see us. He was housed across from the river, Neretva River, where the refugees were housed. Those were people from Dretelj. And this older man came to see us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which ethnicity was this man?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to him or did he speak to you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: He asked where we were from. He told us that he himself was born in Mostar and that before the war he used to work as a judge in Sarajevo and that he was held in the Dretelj camp and upon being released from there was housed in that facility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to take you back a little bit. When you arrived at the village, did your commander, Adnan Solakovic, also arrive at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he eventually come to the village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Yes. He didn't come together with us; however, he did come to the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did he stay in the village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: At the entry point into the village, where there used to be an old railway station which was not in use any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, before, as you said, Celo's soldiers arrived, can you describe the atmosphere in the village, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Well, the atmosphere was peaceful. The villagers who lived there were not very visible. They were moving about seldom. It was very peaceful there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said Celo's soldiers arrived. Can you tell the Court when did they arrive exactly?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: The second day, in the evening, after our arrival.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know which brigade that was?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Maybe I'm going to mix things up. I think it was the 15th Motorised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which corps it belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer. The interpreters didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: They belonged to the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know it was Celo and his soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: That night when they arrived, I didn't know about their arrival. I saw them only in the following morning, when they lined up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in the following morning, how did you know they were Celo's soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: That morning, the unit was lined up. Celo came to visit the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time did he come to visit the unit, roughly?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: At about 10.00 in the morning perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally see him come?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know it was him? Had you seen him before?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: I knew him from before, but not personally. I knew him through television and the papers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you know about him?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about him until a murder occurred in town. Later on it became frequent. It would frequently be reported on television and in the papers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask a few questions about that. When you say "town," which town do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, in Stari Grad, the old town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you hear about that murder or when was that murder allegedly committed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: On the eve of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear about Celo's involvement, if -- if anything, about that murder?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: All we could hear came from the papers and the television; namely, that he was involved in that murder. Nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- while you were in Sarajevo on the front lines, did you hear anything else about Celo and his brigade?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of reputation did they have?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: A bad reputation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by that? Why do you say "bad"?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: At the time, there were several such units, units that could not be placed under the army command. Later on the commanders of those units were removed from posts. The units were disbanded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which units are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Celo's unit, Caco's unit, Delta, and others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what Caco's unit was called?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: The 10th Mountain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said you saw Celo arrive for the line-up the day after you arrived. Did you see him arrive personally?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he arrive?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: He arrived in a jeep, a dark red jeep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then where did he go?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: He went to see the unit that was lined up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the unit lined up?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: A bit further up from the house in which we were billeted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many -- did you see how many soldiers were lined up?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Twenty to thirty soldiers. About that number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far were you from this line-up?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Approximately 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to hear what Celo said to the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: No, we couldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how long he addressed the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: About ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this line-up, did you see anything -- anybody else, apart from military personnel?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that day, did the atmosphere in the village change from when you first arrived? And if it did, how did it change?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: The atmosphere in the village changed after the line-up. Once Celo left, his soldiers started shooting, making a lot of noise. They would occasionally shoot throughout the whole day. So the atmosphere changed completely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, where did they shoot?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: Nothing in particular. They would fire at electricity pylons. Nothing in particular. They would simply fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the shooting would -- they would occasionally shoot throughout the whole day. Could you be more specific? Was the shooting constant? Was the shooting intermittent? Was it sporadic? How would you describe the shooting?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA KADIC
utterances.text: It was intermittent. It wasn't a continuous shooting. But they would fire intermittently throughout the whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps this is a good time.
